component.name: Tin Hat
component.summary: Group chat and calls for game nights

description.p: Tin Hat is a native desktop client for Matrix built around game nights: rooms and spaces, end-to-end encrypted chat, and calls with hardware-encoded, end-to-end encrypted screen sharing.

Calls run on LiveKit through Element Call's protocol, so phones on Element X join the same rooms. Screen shares use NVENC on NVIDIA and VA-API on AMD and Intel, up to 4K at 60 frames per second, with per-person volumes, game chat, pull-aside corners, a soundboard, a Media Party (watch videos and listen to music together) and a squad calendar.

Pad: control a call from another of your devices without joining it, for example your phone as a remote for the call your computer is in. When one of your other devices is in a call, a Pad button shows next to Join (in the room, in Who's around and at the top of the room list). Tap it to play soundboard sounds into the call, stop a sound, mute or unmute, deafen, step away and come back, turn someone's volume up or down, or leave the call, all on the device that is in the call. Pad works only between your own verified devices, and you can turn it off on a device in Settings, Calls, Pad. Tin Hat Web on iPhone and iPad works better, in Safari and from the Home Screen: iOS no longer offers to make up a new password in the Security Key and Start over fields, windows fit an upright iPad, pressing and holding no longer starts a text selection, the keyboard no longer covers the sign-in or what you type, and buttons are easier to tap. Tin Hat Web also opens rooms of the newest room version, which some other servers make. Also: the Security Key hint in Verify this device no longer points to a settings page that doesn't exist; it now says the key is the one you saved when you first set up encryption, so look where you keep it.

Lost your Security Key and have no other device signed in? You can now start over: in Verify this device, choose No other device? Use your Security Key, then Lost your Security Key? Start over. Tin Hat checks your password first and changes nothing if it is wrong; then your account gets a new Security Key to save. Messages from before stay locked unless a device that still has them signs in again, and people who verified you will see that your security changed. Also: importing your Steam library (and searching games, and their pictures) works right after you sign in, instead of only after restarting Tin Hat.

Tin Hat now works with any Tin Hat server: your own, or one a friend runs. Type its address when you sign in; the app asks that server what it offers and shows only that, and your calls, uploads and problem reports go to that server alone. The guest room: let people in for a while without an account. Turn it on in Settings, Guests and share the guest link; when someone knocks, the Guests room shows who is waiting and you let them in or turn them away. Forgot your password? On a server that sends no email, the sign-in screen tells you to ask the person who runs it for a new one, and you can now change your own password any time in Settings, Devices and security, Change password. Updates now come from GitHub. Signing out now ends your call first and forgets the account on that computer: the device is signed out on the server, and the messages and files it kept are removed (your device settings stay). Also: every person and room keeps one colour everywhere, accepting a DM invite opens the DM, a pasted invite link fills in the code, and a message this device cannot read says why.

Same room: two of you on two devices in one room? Link up. Tin Hat then sends one voice from your room (the mic that hears the talker loudest) and your devices stop playing each other, so nobody else hears either of you twice or hears their own voice come back. Link up from the same-room pill or right-click a tile; people you have linked with link up again by themselves next time (Settings, Audio, Same room). Media Party: Watch Party grew up - a Media Party button right on the call bar with a now-playing strip, a polished player (fullscreen, shortcuts, buffering and clear errors), a queue you can reorder and clear, who is watching, and a browse pane: search YouTube with filters and suggestions, YouTube Music songs and playlists (add a whole playlist at once), Trending, and the room History. Spotify and Apple Music links turn into song cards that play their YouTube match for everyone.

On Windows, Backspace works again in every text box. Since 10.8 it closed the open window instead of deleting a letter (the problem report closed at the first typo), and with the room list folded away it opened the list. If Tin Hat crashes on Windows, its log now says where, so crashes can be tracked down.

Settings is now its own window: every setting sits in clear cards, a search box jumps straight to what you need, your profile has one Save button, Devices and security are in one place, and a new About and help page holds updates, the tour and shortcuts. The main menu is down to Settings, Edit layout, Theme, About and Sign out. The plus button above your rooms starts a new DM (just type their username) or, inside a space, a new room. New accounts set up their encryption on their first device and show their Security Key once, instead of asking to be verified by another device. Your status popup has a Profile settings button.

New widgets: Polls (ask a question in a room and see the votes; Element users can vote too) and Game night (plan a night, see who is coming and spin the Game Reel), from the main menu with Add widget. The widget gallery no longer covers widget names with its Preview label. On Windows, switches that are off are now visible in light themes.

New widgets, from the main menu with Add widget: Game servers (what is running, who is on and the join address; admins can start, stop or restart), Pinned messages, Mentions from every room, a Sticky note per space, Is it just me (checks your connection and your server), Memories (your latest recordings), a Dice roller with history, Friend clocks (the local time of each friend; you can stop sharing yours in Settings) and a Soundboard pad. On Windows, switches that are on now look on, and the right-click volume menu on a call tile opens where you click, with working sliders. On KDE, a mouse wheel step on a volume dial now saves.

Ctrl+K lists your pending invites again: they come first before you type, with the same Invited pill as the room list, and Enter shows the invite in the room list, ready to accept. Ctrl+K also finds the people you have direct chats with. The Theme menu in the main menu has a new last row, Edit current theme, which opens the theme editor on the theme you are using. In a call, a new pin at the end of the call buttons keeps them on screen instead of letting them hide a few seconds after you stop moving the mouse. The same choice is in Settings, Calls, as Keep call buttons visible, and in Ctrl+K.

Tin Hat no longer keeps a CPU core busy on Windows while the This device is not verified banner shows, and the banner no longer leaves an empty band under it. The update banner no longer makes Tin Hat lag on Windows either.

Make Tin Hat yours. Edit mode (Ctrl+E, or right-click any gap) lets you drag every island where you want it, dock them side by side or stack them as tabs, resize the gaps, and hide what you don't use. Start from a preset: Classic, Compact, Call-first, Side monitor or Handheld. Your layouts follow you to every device, and Settings > Appearance > Layout can always reset one. Every button row is yours too: hide, reorder and add buttons, make your own button islands (join a room's call, play a sound, open a room, set a status, switch theme), press Ctrl+K to run anything, and give any action a keyboard shortcut. The theme editor builds your own colours on top of any theme, with a Pick tool that edits anything you click, and you can share a theme into a room for friends to try or keep. Also: Call stats no longer shows how long people spent in calls.
Tin Hat keeps updating on a side screen while you play: the GPU saving for when its window isn't focused is now an option in Settings (off by default), for lower-end PCs.

Islands. Every part of the window now floats as its own rounded island: the nav buttons, DMs, spaces, rooms, you, the room header, the call, the conversation, the message box and the room info. Prefer the old look? Settings > Appearance > Layout > Flat puts everything edge to edge again, on that device. New widgets under the room list: Up next (your next events, answer in place), Call stats (how well you hear each person, and how well they hear you) and Who's around. The settings button next to your name now lists your five most recent themes. Tin Hat is much lighter: nothing redraws while it sits idle, GIFs play three times and then rest, and while its window isn't focused a call shows cameras small at 15 frames a second (both can be changed in Settings). Long calls use far less memory and fewer threads.

Themes are here. Settings > Appearance has nearly 1,200 colour themes to pick from, dark or light: Dracula, Nord, Catppuccin, Gruvbox, Solarized, Rose Pine, Tokyo Night and many more. You can also import your own from iTerm2, kitty, Alacritty, Ghostty, WezTerm, Windows Terminal, Xresources or base16. Your theme follows you to every device, Tin Hat Web included, or you can give one device its own. Text stays readable in every theme. The call sounds and the icon style are now their own settings.
Tin Hat on Windows no longer opens in Safe mode every second start. Verifying a new sign-in with emoji works again, also with the Element apps.

Unread DMs now sit at the top of the rail, and new DMs and invites notify you. Presence is here, off until you turn it on: friends see Online, Away or In a call, plus gaming statuses in their own colours (click your name at the bottom-left). Replies now notify the person you replied to, and badges only count what matters.

Echo cancellation works whichever speaker the call plays on (no need to pick the output by hand). Going back into a busy room shows the conversation again. Game Reel: admins can reset tonight's spins and undo credit (reset all, per person or per spin), plus a "Spins affect credits" switch for free spins. Also fixes a rare audio lag.

Echo cancellation works whichever speaker the call plays on (no need to pick the output by hand). Going back into a busy room shows the conversation again. Game Reel: admins can reset tonight's spins and undo credit (reset all, per person or per spin), plus a "Spins affect credits" switch for free spins.

Fewer notification chimes during calls. Game Reel works for any number of people, and spins save again. Tin Hat now talks to its server's new web address. The Windows installer closes a running Tin Hat first.

Can they hear me? A small pill in the call header now says when your microphone sends nothing at all (judged on the raw microphone, so a noise gate or a quiet room no longer trips it), when it is muted or at 0 % in your system's sound settings (one click fixes it), when your speakers are, and when the call isn't getting your mic. Talking while muted shows a "You're muted" reminder above the mic button, with an optional sound in Settings, Calls. Hover the mic button to see who is receiving you: every Tin Hat in the call reports what it hears. Tiles mark who is deafened, who isn't receiving you, and whom you can't hear (click to repair). Echo: Tin Hat notices when someone's microphone sends your own voice back and tells them, and when your own mic picks up your speakers (the call or a game), with one click to turn on echo cancellation. Also: a failed audio setting change, reconnect or first playback no longer leaves you silent or deaf, and push-to-talk starts muted.

Call security and stability: media keys sent by other people can no longer replace your own call key; the app no longer posts call keys into the room timeline, which also ends the notification chime every few minutes during a long call in an encrypted room; cancelling a stuck join can no longer close a call you joined afterwards; hanging up no longer freezes when a camera driver stops responding.

Fixes voices going silent a few minutes into a call on some Linux machines (the audio server dropped the app's playback stream). Playback now heals itself the way the microphone already did: the output is rebuilt on the same audio path, then the other one, and the app keeps trying instead of giving up.

Space tags. A role now shows on people: their name takes the role's colour and the role sits as a tag next to it, in chat, in the member list and on the profile card, in every room of the space. The member list groups people by role (each role can opt out in its settings). The Roles editor keeps Create, Save and Delete in view under the form instead of at the end of the permissions list. Video embeds in chat (YouTube and the like) go full screen from the player's own button; Esc comes back. Invite codes: server admins get an Invites tab in Settings to make, copy and revoke codes, and the sign-in screen gains "Create an account" that turns a code into an account.

Notifications are part of the chat again. Rooms set to All messages no longer chime or count "missed messages" for people joining or leaving a call, calendar changes or other room housekeeping: only real messages count, on every client of your account. Reading to the bottom of a room clears its badge even when the newest thing in it is a call join, and a floating chat bubble counts as reading while the main window is behind a call. Settings: a new Notifications tab holds desktop alerts and every sound; Never record me moved to Privacy.

Roles and moderation. Spaces get a settings window (right-click a space, the gear in the room list header, or Ctrl+Shift+comma): name, photo, topic and who can join; every member with search, invite, kick and ban; named roles with colours, ranks and permissions that Tin Hat applies to every room in the space; and the rooms with their sync state. In a call, right-click someone for Moderation: mute their mic for everyone, disconnect them, kick or ban them from the space. Invited spaces show in the rail with a Join / Decline card.

Fixes a crash in the Flatpak when opening the audio settings or picking a speaker or microphone during a call: device lists no longer restart PipeWire's device scanner on every open, which is where the sandbox's GStreamer PipeWire plugin fell over.

The bottom row lines up: the account footer floats as a rounded card level with the rail's + and the message box, the rooms fade out beneath it, and the message box sits down with them. The typing notice moved above the message box.
Update now inside the Flatpak installs the new version at once instead of waiting for Flatpak's half-hourly check, shows the download progress, and Restart relaunches straight into it.

The polish release: room info and members dock beside the chat with invited and banned people listed; Mark as read on rooms and spaces; a window-wide strip for the verify, offline and update banners; pins that survive the scrollback; spoilers stay hidden; the emoji picker stays open; the call bar fits and voice tiles wrap instead of shrinking; the game reel ticks and lands with a payoff; the watch party has a host; Appearance gains Reduce motion and a 12/24-hour clock; and about a hundred smaller sandings.

Audio in the Flatpak diagnoses and heals itself: streams carry their own volume and routing so a remembered mute or route can no longer silence them, a playback that stops draining switches audio API on its own, every audio start and stop is bounded so the app cannot freeze on a stuck stream, and the log records what PipeWire sees of the app's streams. The emoji, GIF and pinned-message popups open inside the window.
The Flatpak plays other people's audio through PulseAudio-compat by default, matching the microphone path; you can hear the call again on desktops where the sandbox's PipeWire plugin stays silent.
The Flatpak captures the microphone and the echo-cancel reference through PulseAudio-compat by default, and hanging up can no longer hang on a stuck capture.

Audio device lists no longer come up empty in the Flatpak, and a microphone that PipeWire's older plugin cannot read falls back to the PulseAudio path; the chat scroll bar shows only while scrolling or hovering its edge and no longer covers messages; the message box sits centred between the divider and the window edge.
In-app updates work inside the Flatpak: the update monitor is registered at start, and Update now installs as soon as Flatpak has seen the new version, or tells you the one command to run.

Calls join again in the Flatpak (the microphone pipeline named a PipeWire property the runtime does not have); dragging a space to reorder it no longer shows the file-drop overlay; the message box sits on the bottom edge.
Tin Hat: the app's new name, now a Flatpak with a new mark, new sounds, notification and call sounds, and an incoming-call toast.
